segments.voice: Yesterday, we left the Rudram where it lives: chanted while water pours over the stone. Now the night.
screen: `THE RUDRAM, POURED OVER STONE.` · `NOW THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Diwali fills a night with lamps. Holi fills a morning with color. Maha Shivaratri asks for something stranger. Don't eat. Don't sleep. Stay up in the dark, through the hours when the house goes quiet, and keep your attention on one thing until the sky starts to gray. No fireworks. The reward, if there is one, comes at dawn, to someone tired and hungry and still there. You've met this night through its stories: the hunter in the tree, the pillar of fire. This week we take the night itself as a course of study.
screen: `DON'T EAT. DON'T SLEEP.` → `ATTENTION ON ONE THING TILL DAWN.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF, AS A COURSE.`

segments.voice: The name says it plainly. Maha, great. Shiva. Ratri, night. Tradition places it in the dark half of the lunar month, on the night just before the new moon, when there's almost no moon to see by. The Shiva Purana describes a vow for this night. Fast through the day. Worship Shiva in the linga, with water and bilva leaves. Stay awake until morning. That's the whole syllabus, short enough to fit on a card. But notice what kind of teaching it is. Nobody hands you a book or gives a lecture. The night teaches through the body. Hunger is one lesson, sleepiness another, the dark a third. Each takes away something you usually lean on, food, rest, light, and asks what's left to lean on instead. Some readers hear the near-moonless sky that way too: the mind's usual light gone, and only one thing worth turning toward. So we'll go through the night in order: the morning vow, the fast, keeping awake, the name repeated in the dark, the offerings, and dawn. One piece a day. Some people keep every hour in a temple crowded until sunrise. Some keep part of it at home. Some only learn about it. The course is the same either way. Its first lesson: the night isn't an empty space between two days. On this night, the night is the point.
screen: `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `FAST, WORSHIP, STAY AWAKE.` · `THE NIGHT TEACHES THROUGH THE BODY.` · `ONE PIECE OF THE NIGHT A DAY.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Dim the light around you if you can, or simply close your eyes, and notice what the dark takes away, the screen, the faces, and what it gives back: sounds you hadn't heard, the weight of your body, the breath. Keep your attention on one thing, the breath is enough, and come back to it whenever you drift. If you pray, you can hold Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as that one thing.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, taken this week as a night curriculum. Today, its shape: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. The dark takes things away, and gives some back. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep it may fast, visit Shiva temples or worship at home, offer water, milk and bilva leaves to the linga, and stay awake through the night with chanting and singing.

notes: First of seven Shivaratri days (1153–1159). Plan for the week, one piece of the night per day: shape (1153), the vow/sankalpa (1154), the fast (1155, week end), keeping awake (1156), the name through the night (1157), the offerings (1158), dawn and breaking the fast (1159, close of the Shiva part). The hunter and the pillar of fire were told in years 1–4 already, so they are only named here.
The index word is cut off ('Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum'); kept exactly as required. Suggest the outline give this run a proper word (e.g. 'Maha Shivaratri' or 'jagarana').

Calendar: Maha Shivaratri falls on the chaturdashi of the krishna paksha (Magha by the amanta reckoning, Phalguna by the purnimanta). Stated only as 'the dark half of the lunar month, the night just before the new moon', attributed to tradition; confirm.
Confirm the Shiva Purana location of the Shivaratri vrata (Koti Rudra Samhita; also Vidyeshvara Samhita) and that fasting, linga worship with bilva and water, and keeping awake are all in it.
'Some readers' reading of the near-moonless night as the mind without its usual light is offered as interpretation, not doctrine.
